finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so this is a first build. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2017 Corolla about $246-$413 (0.6-1 hr); midsize 2017 Accord about $164-$302 (0.6-1 hr); truck 2021 F-150 about $164-$290 (0.7-1 hr); luxury 2015 Lexus ES 350 has no low end, because the lower labor time for that class is null, and tops out at about $518 (list-price motor and 1 hour); if the 0.6 hour that two luxury-make cross-checks point to were used, its low end would be about $334, but that figure is not built in. A supportable range for mainstream vehicles is therefore about $165-$415. The two general benchmarks sit inside or just above that: FIXD $297-$352 is inside it, and YourMechanic's Blazer examples ($308-$425 mobile, up to $693 at a shop) reach above it. RepairPal's BMW X6 figure ($899-$1,118) is far above our luxury ceiling, which shows that large European luxury vehicles, where the motor comes with its linkage or sits deep under the cowl, can cost about double the example here; no parts were loaded for one, so the luxury figures should be read as a Japanese luxury sedan only. Parts: every high is a genuine list price from a dealer catalog page for the example vehicle and year ($252.81 Corolla, $142.38 Accord, $130.18 F-150, $357.60 ES 350). Every low is the lowest verified discounted price of the same genuine motor, not an aftermarket price, because no new aftermarket motor naming an example vehicle and year was found on a page that would load; the only new aftermarket motors seen ($128-$132) printed no fitment. Aftermarket motors probably exist for these cars and could bring the low ends down. The luxury class still has a single parts source: further searches on the Lexus part number returned only the same seller, used-parts yards and marketplace listings. How solid the labor times are, stated plainly. Low ends: three are a manufacturer's warranty time printed with the unit for replacing the wiper motor alone, but only the truck's is for the example vehicle (Ford 0.7 Hours, 2021-2022 F-150). The economy and midsize lows are Mitsubishi's 0.6 hours for the 2011-2015 Outlander Sport and the 2007-2013 Outlander, comparable vehicles and not the examples. The luxury low is now null: the only luxury-make times found are FCA's 0.6 hours for the 2018 Alfa Romeo Stelvio, where the motor and linkage are replaced as one unit, and GM's 0.6 for the 2014 Cadillac CTS wiper module, printed with no unit; both include the linkage, so both are cross-checks. Hyundai's 0.5 M/H for the 2011-2013 Equus is for the motor's cover, not the motor. No Toyota, Honda, Lexus, Acura or Infiniti time with a unit for the motor was found; Honda's and Acura's recent wiper motor notices to dealers print no time. An older Dodge Ram recall allows only 0.4 hours for the motor alone, so some trucks are quicker than the F-150. Warranty times are the low end of what shops bill. High ends: every class uses 1 hour, now from two general sources that are not for any example vehicle: a named technician's guide saying the job should take about an hour and that a qualified mechanic will not need more than an hour when the motor is easy to reach, and a parts maker's tip sheet printing a replacement time of under 1 hour for a service technician. A maker cross-check agrees: Ford allows 0.8 Hours (Bronco Sport, Maverick) and 1.0 Hours (Mustang Mach-E) to take out the linkage, check the motor's date code and replace the motor, a time that includes the inspection. Neither high is a flat-rate book time. The only book-time figure seen is second-hand: a question-and-answer post quoting a labor guide at 0.8 hr for a 2003 Accord. Figures above 1 hour exist but are weak: an unsigned seller guide says 1 to 1.5 hours for a do-it-yourselfer, FIXD says 30 to 90 minutes (another estimator, so not used), and a question-and-answer post puts an old BMW 5 Series at about 2 hours; a shop that bills 1.5 hours would add about $60-$80 to the high ends above. Because one labor end is null, three classes rest on times that are not for the example vehicle and the luxury class has one parts source, confidence is low. This is an estimate, never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds diagnosis (a dead wiper can be a fuse, relay, switch, control module or seized linkage, not the motor), shop supplies and sales tax. The wiper linkage (transmission) is often worn or seized when the motor fails and may be quoted with it; on some vehicles the motor is sold only with the linkage, which raises the part price (on the 2021 F-150 the assembly with linkage lists at $434.55 against $130.18 for the motor alone). New wiper blades or arms, a cowl panel clip or seal broken on removal, and the rear wiper motor are separate.
